title.en: Technical Writing for Data and AI Work
title.ar: الكتابة التقنية لأعمال البيانات والذكاء الاصطناعي

tagline: Write the README, decision memo, experiment report and model card a data or AI project runs on, for a named reader, with every claim checked
description: Participants write the documents that data and AI work runs on: a README, a design document, a decision memo, an experiment report and a model or system card. Each starts from a repository, a model comparison or an evaluation log and ends with a peer test; one draft is unassisted, another is revised with an assistant, and every claim is checked.
audience: Beginners. Graduates, career changers and computing professionals preparing for Developer or Specialist courses, who can run a Python notebook but have not yet studied AI methods.
prerequisites: Has a small data or code project, own or provided, to document

outcomes.text: Identify the reader, purpose and required sections of five common technical document types, given five scenarios with named readers
outcomes.evidence: an outline per scenario matching the reference structure

outcomes.text: Draft a README that lets a stranger install, run and check a small project, given an undocumented repository
outcomes.evidence: the README and a peer's run log on a clean environment

outcomes.text: Draft a one-page decision memo with options, trade-offs, a recommendation and the conditions that would change it, given a measured comparison of two models on quality, cost and latency
outcomes.evidence: a memo scored on a five-criterion rubric

outcomes.text: Prepare an experiment report and a model card that state uncertainty, results by data slice and known limits, given an evaluation run log
outcomes.evidence: a report and card that pass a peer checklist

outcomes.text: Compare an unassisted draft with an assisted revision for accuracy, clarity and invented content, given the participant's two drafts
outcomes.evidence: a revision log of how each claim was checked

case_study.name: Tarthuth Veterinary Clinics
case_study.summary: A fictional private chain of veterinary clinics whose two-person data team built a small Python project, the request urgency tagger, that sorts owners' appointment messages in Arabic, English and mixed text into urgent, soon and routine. Every file is synthetic and generated with a fixed seed: the messages, a 400-message test set, the outputs of a keyword-rules baseline that really runs, the simulated and recorded outputs of two hosted models labelled Model S and Model L with their cost and latency, and the evaluation log. No model was called.

format_note: Workshop: one and a half days of writing labs and a tracked follow-up review

days.title: Writing for a reader

sessions.title: Write for one reader
sessions.summary: Name the reader and the decision before choosing the document, then put the bottom line first
outcomes: Name the reader, purpose and decision behind a request for a document
Choose the document type and its required sections for a scenario
Rewrite an update so the bottom line, the request and the uncertainty come first

lab.title: Bottom-line-first rewrite
lab.summary: Outline five documents for five readers, then rewrite the data team's status update bottom line first and check it

steps.text: Read the five scenarios and name each reader's decision
Outline the five documents: reader, purpose, sections
Mark where the status update hides its bottom line
Rewrite it bottom line first, with glossary terms and uncertainty in words
Run the checker, then score a partner's rewrite with the rubric

lab.stretch: Write the first paragraph again in Arabic with the glossary's Arabic terms

sessions.title: READMEs, designs and decisions
sessions.summary: Write what a stranger needs to install, run and check a project, and keep designs and decisions as text beside the code
outcomes: Write install, run and check steps a stranger can follow on a clean machine
Separate a README from a design document and a decision record
Draw a pipeline as text that the repository renders

lab.title: Peer-tested README
lab.summary: Write the README of the undocumented urgency tagger, test it with a clean run, then have a partner follow it and log the run

steps.text: Explore the repository and list what a stranger would have to guess
Write the install, run and check sections
Add the purpose, inputs and outputs, limits and a text diagram
Run the clean-run test on your README and fix what fails
Swap: a partner follows your README on a clean copy and writes the run log

lab.stretch: Start the README of your own project, the first part of the capstone

sessions.title: The decision memo
sessions.summary: Turn a measured comparison into one page: options, trade-offs, a recommendation and what would change it
outcomes: State the decision and the recommendation in the first two sentences
Compare options on quality, cost and latency with numbers traced to the source
Write the conditions under which the recommendation would change

lab.title: Decision memo
lab.summary: Write a one-page memo to the operations director on which tagger the reception desk should use, from the measured comparison

steps.text: Read the context and the comparison; write the decision in one line
Write the bottom line and the three options
Write the trade-offs with numbers from the comparison and their intervals
Write the recommendation and the conditions that would change it
Run the checker; a partner scores your memo on the five-criterion rubric

lab.stretch: Write the same choice as a decision record under five headings

days.subtitle: One reader, the bottom line first, and the documents a project needs before anyone else can use it

days.title: Evidence documents and writing with assistance

sessions.title: Experiment reports and model cards
sessions.summary: Report what an evaluation measured, by slice and with its uncertainty, and write the card a user of the model reads
outcomes: Report results by data slice with the number of cases and an interval
Write known limits and out-of-scope uses a reader can act on
Check a report and a card with a peer checklist

lab.title: Experiment report and model card
lab.summary: From the evaluation log, write an experiment report for the data team lead and a model card for the head of reception, the report drafted with AI off

steps.text: Run the statistics tool on the evaluation log and read the slice table
Draft the experiment report with AI off: question, setup, results, uncertainty
Draft the model card for the head of reception
Run the card checker and fix what it reports
Swap with a partner and complete the peer checklist

lab.stretch: Add a text diagram of the evaluation flow to the report

sessions.title: Writing with an assistant
sessions.summary: Draft without the assistant first, then check every claim an assisted revision changes, log it and disclose it
outcomes: Spot the typical errors of an assisted revision: changed numbers, dropped limits, invented sources
Keep a revision log that says how each claim was checked
Write a disclosure line and a context file for a coding agent

lab.title: Unassisted draft against assisted revision
lab.summary: Compare your AI-off report with an assisted revision claim by claim, keep a revision log, disclose the assistance and write the repository's agent context file

steps.text: Produce the assisted revision of your draft
Run the claim diff
Check each changed claim and log it
Write the final version and its disclosure line
Write the agent context file for the tagger
Run the log checker and fix it

lab.stretch: Revise with an approved assistant on Public text only, and log it the same way

days.subtitle: Reports and cards that state uncertainty, slices and limits, and an assistant whose every change is checked

days.title: Documentation set review
days.subtitle: Each participant shows the set in four minutes, then answers four minutes of questions on its claims and its history

capstone.summary: A documentation set for one project (README, decision memo, model or system card, revision log), reviewed in a follow-up
capstone.submission: An individual task, submitted as a public GitHub repository link before the follow-up review. The repository holds the project or a link to it, the README, the decision memo, the model or system card, the revision log with its disclosure line, and the commit history that shows the drafts. Only public or synthetic material is used, and only Public text goes to any assistant.

rubric.criterion: The README lets a stranger install, run and check the project on a clean machine
The decision memo states options, trade-offs, a recommendation and the conditions that would change it
The card states intended use, results by slice with uncertainty, and known limits
The revision log shows how each assisted change was checked, with a disclosure line
Each document is written for its named reader: bottom line first, consistent terms, plain uncertainty
